svg.text: A fenced write is one transaction: check the token, then write
Step 1 must touch exactly one row; if it doesn't, the whole transaction is rolled back.
One transaction (atomic)
Step 1 · check the token (must affect exactly 1 row)
UPDATE bcs_task_leases SET write_seq = write_seq + 1
WHERE env = ? AND session_id = ? AND fencing_token = :mine
verifies the token AND takes the lease-row lock
Step 2…n · the durable writes for this session
run status · node-run progress · checkpoints · history
dispatch / delivery records (item 3) · durable timers
all in the same database as the lease row
Token matches
step 1 touches 1 row → steps run → COMMIT
write_seq always changes, so the count is 1
(a no-op SET x = x would report 0 rows)
write_seq also tells a handoff successor what changed
Token is stale (someone claimed S)
step 1 touches 0 rows → whole transaction rolls back
caller gets LeaseLost →
stop driving S, evict it, never retry
Why a concurrent claim can't slip in between check and commit
A claim (or a handoff transfer) also updates the lease row, so it needs the same row lock. It waits until the fenced transaction commits,
then bumps the token. Every later fenced write by the old owner fails step 1. Check and write are never separated by a gap a pause can fall into.
Rules: same transaction · same database · one session per transaction · LeaseLost means stop · unknown commit outcome → read back, never blind-retry.
